title: Old model or new model?
scenario: Lantern Studio wants to test image models for Fernhill Candles. You judge the shortlist, the test set-up and the results, using the exhibit. The job mix, the plan, the usage and the results are made up for this case. The vendor lines are copied from the docs.
exhibit:
JOB MIX (made up for this case)
  70% edits of approved packshots (change a label, move a candle).
  30% new social images.
  Most jobs send 2 to 4 reference images.

VENDOR LINES (copied from the docs)
  OpenAI: "Choose Sunburst for workflows where editing precision matters most,
    and Flare for fast, high-quality everyday image generation."
  Google, Nano Banana Pro: "The premium choice for the most complex visual tasks".
  Google, Nano Banana 2 Lite: "Not optimized for multiple reference inputs or
    multi-turn sequential editing."

TEST PLAN (made up)
  Model X (current): quality = high.   Model Y (new): quality = auto.
  Same 50 jobs, same prompts, same rubric.

REVIEW SET-UP (made up)
  Files: model-x_017.png and model-y_017.png. X is always on the left.

USAGE FROM THE API RESPONSE (made up)
  Model X: 4,000 output tokens per image, on average.
  Model Y: 5,000 output tokens per image, on average.
  Rate for both: $30 per 1,000,000 output tokens. Ignore text input.

BLIND RESULT (made up)
  100 pairs.  Model Y preferred: 54.  Model X preferred: 46.  No ties.

questions.prompt: Which shortlist of two models fits the job mix best?

options.text: Flare and Nano Banana 2 Lite, because both are described as fast and cheap for daily work
options.explanation: Most jobs are edits with several references. The Gemini API docs say Lite is not optimized for that.

options.text: Sunburst and Nano Banana 2 Lite, because Sunburst edits well and Lite is the cheapest
options.explanation: Lite is not optimized for multiple reference inputs or sequential editing, and most jobs use both.

options.text: Sunburst and Nano Banana Pro, since the vendor lines tie them to editing and hard tasks
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI picks Sunburst for editing precision, and the Gemini API docs call Pro the choice for the most complex tasks. These are vendor claims, so the test still decides.

options.text: Flare and Nano Banana Pro, because Flare is for everyday images and most jobs are everyday
options.explanation: 70% of the jobs are edits of approved packshots, where the OpenAI docs point to Sunburst.

questions.prompt: What is the main problem with the test plan?

options.text: Model X runs at high quality and Y at auto, so a gap may come from the setting, not the model
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI docs say `auto` lets the model choose the setting. Fix quality and size for both, so only the model differs.

options.text: Both models run on the same 50 jobs, which makes the test unfair to the older model here
options.explanation: Using the same jobs is what makes the comparison fair.

options.text: The test uses the same rubric for both models, so it cannot show any real difference at all
options.explanation: One rubric for both is what lets the scores be compared.

options.text: It has only 50 jobs, while any A/B test of image models needs at least 400 to start
options.explanation: The Anthropic engineering post says a large effect can be seen with a small sample, and small effects need more. There is no 400 rule.

questions.prompt: The file names show the model, and X is always on the left. What is the fix?

options.text: Tell reviewers to ignore the names and always trust their first look at each pair
options.explanation: A reminder does not remove the clue. The OpenAI docs describe a randomized, blinded test.

options.text: Always put the new model on the left, since it is the one that is being tested
options.explanation: A fixed side keeps the position effect on one model. The sides should be random.

options.text: Ask only the art director to review, since one person cannot be swayed by file names
options.explanation: A single reviewer can still be swayed by a name or a side.

options.text: Rename files Left and Right, hide the models, and flip a coin for each job's sides
options.explanation: Right. This matches OpenAI's randomized, blinded human test.

questions.prompt: Using the usage numbers, what does one image cost on each model?

options.text: Both cost $0.12 per image, because both models share the same rate per token
options.explanation: The OpenAI docs say equal token rates do not mean equal cost per image. Model Y used more tokens.

options.text: X costs $0.12 and Y costs $0.15, so the same rate gave different bills
X costs $0.012 and Y costs $0.015, because the rate in the exhibit is per million tokens
options.explanation: That is a decimal slip. 4,000 tokens is 0.4% of a million, and 0.004 x $30 = $0.12.

options.text: Both cost $0.15 per image, because the price follows the heavier of the two models
options.explanation: Each model is billed on its own tokens. X used 4,000, not 5,000.

questions.prompt: What should the studio report about the blind result of 54 to 46?

options.text: Model Y wins, because it was preferred in more pairs and the vendor said it is better
options.explanation: A gap of 8 pairs in 100 is small. A vendor's claim is not a test result.

options.text: Model X wins, because it is the current model and a tie should always go to it
options.explanation: Nobody wrote a rule like that. The rule should be set before the run.

options.text: The gap is small: call it about even, test more pairs, or let cost and gates decide
options.explanation: Right. The Anthropic engineering post says small effects need larger evals. Our rule: treat a small gap as a tie, and write the rule before the run.

options.text: The test is void, because a blind test cannot be used when only two models are compared
options.explanation: A blind pair test works well with two models. The result is just not decisive.
